A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we are exploring the ways in which socially engaged documentary practices in East Asia represent a form of “vernacular modernism,” in which the modern is not simply the enemy, but is instead the site of a struggle over how to live in the present.

the films of these three directors are all about the evocation of another world, a world in which the values of community participation and the defense of local culture are placed above the imperatives of capital accumulation and the demands of globalized modernity.

we have sought to demonstrate how socially engaged documentary practices have emerged as a means to reorient documentary practice toward the needs of the communities it represents, while also seeking to recalibrate the terms of modernity itself.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in a world increasingly shaped by global capital, the notion of a socially engaged documentary mode is a vital one, and one that is likely to become more important, not less, in the future.

the socially engaged mode of documentary is not simply a response to the pressures of globalization; it is also a response to the ways in which the modernity that globalization brings is itself being reimagined in East Asia.

the notion of socially engaged documentary is useful insofar as it helps us to understand a particular set of documentary practices in East Asia that have been developed in the context of the region’s own particular history of modernity.
